big_case_rationale: A recurring, decades-old FRCP question touching everyday civil litigation in every district court, but technical and low-salience outside the procedure bar; the underlying employment dispute is individual, not systemic.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority rests the judgment on the text and structure of Rules 8(c), 15, and 16 read together: Rule 8(c)(1)'s command that a party must affirmatively state any affirmative defense cannot be satisfied by raising an unpleaded defense for the first time in a summary-judgment motion under the Eleventh Circuit's prejudice-only Hassan test, because that end-run nullifies Rule 15(a)(2)'s leave requirement and Rule 16(b)(4)'s good-cause bar; a late defense must instead be channeled through the amendment rules, with the summary-judgment motion construed at most as a motion to amend judged on the Rule 15/16 standards.

The majority states its rule categorically and trans-substantively — one standard governing unpleaded affirmative defenses in all federal civil cases, not a holding confined to Title VII's personal-staff exemption or to these parties' facts — while stopping short of per se forfeiture: it channels late defenses through the Rule 15/16 amendment standards rather than declaring them waived outright, and it remands for application of that standard rather than directing judgment for the plaintiff.
